Read the status only and send no DATA
Multiplex streams to scan internal ports over one connection

reports.mechanic: Origin-only path delimiters (`;` in Spring, `.` in Rails, `%00` in OpenLiteSpeed, `%0a` in nginx) plus normalization gaps give both web cache deception and arbitrary cache poisoning through key normalization ("Cache-What-Where").

`/homeabcd` differs; `/home$abcd` matching R0 proves `$` is an origin delimiter
Compare `GET /home/index?cacheBuster` against `/aaa/../home/index?cacheBuster` to see who normalizes
Intruder over all ASCII raw and encoded; the cache buster is the safety mechanism

`/share/%2F..%2Fapi/auth/session?cachebuster=<unique>` against your own session, the unique buster guaranteeing no other user's entry is touched
Retrieve the cached session response

Check whether the reflected value swallows the intervening pairs instead of returning just `start`
Chain a WAF-bypassing reflected XSS plus a credentialed-CORS Tomcat subdomain reflector to read the HttpOnly cookie

Read the SMTP envelope to see which domain the MTA resolved

Escalate to argument injection, traversal or RCE through the spawned tool

Normalization after validation turns it into a UNC path
Observe the inbound SMB connection to your own Responder-style listener (OOB, check program policy first)

Send characters that normalize into the dangerous form afterwards

Find the input the two read differently

reports.first_signal: `(1/0).zxy.zxy` errors in any supported language and the error text identifies it; the blind pairs `(3*4/2)` versus `3*)2(/4` and `((7*8)/(2*4))` versus `7)(*)8)(2/(*4` where a response difference proves evaluation without running a command; polyglot `${{<%[%'"}}%\.`
reports.mechanic: Error-based SSTI forces an error whose message echoes attacker data or command output, and boolean error-based blind raises an error only when a condition is false, so no time delay is needed.
chain: Send the polyglot, then `(1/0).zxy.zxy` to identify the language from the error text
Send the arithmetic pairs, keeping true and false payloads minimally different to exclude WAF and proxy noise

Use the per-language error sink: Python `getattr("", OUTPUT)` or `{% include OUTPUT %}`, PHP `call_user_func(OUTPUT)`, SpEL `Integer.valueOf(OUTPUT)`, OGNL `OUTPUT/0`, Freemarker `?new()`, Ruby `File.read(OUTPUT)`, Node `require(OUTPUT)`, Elixir `[1,2][OUTPUT]`, prefixing output with `Y:/A:/` so it can never accidentally resolve and suppress the error
Baseline comparison over status, length, word and line counts, headers, cookies, redirects, final URL, Content-Type and Server, stable within 5%, discarding the first request
reports.impact_proof: Output recovery on previously blind sinks: expr-eval (CVE-2025-13204), JSONPath Plus (CVE-2025-1302), Twig sandbox CVE-2022-23614, Dust.JS. Toolkit SSTImap 1.3.0 or newer.

reports.first_signal: Filter params naming both a field AND an operator (`q=email=~elttam.com`); keys containing `__` (Django/Beego relational traversal `created_by__user__username__contains`); list/search endpoints accepting arbitrary field names; OData `/$metadata` plus `$filter`/`$expand`; endpoints accepting a nested object where a string is expected (`resetToken[not]=E` via `express.urlencoded({extended:true})`, `j:`-prefixed JSON cookies)
reports.mechanic: A user-controlled filter field and operator reach the ORM, giving a boolean, error or timing oracle over fields that are never meant to be searchable, such as password, salt and token.
chain: Filter on a harmless field for a baseline
Add an unexpected field or operator, or send an object where a string is expected
Observe the change in result count, length, error or timing; collation matters because MySQL/MariaDB/SQLite/MSSQL are case-insensitive by default
reports.impact_proof: Harbor password hashes plus salts (CVE-2025-30086, with two patch bypasses: `email__password__startswith`, then the `=~` fuzzy syntax appending `__icontains`); Prisma reset-token bypass into ATO; Directus CVE-2025-64748; EF dynamic-LINQ and OData full token leak. Tools: `plormber` for timing, elttam semgrep rules.

Reproduce locally (PoC github.com/roaris/CVE-2024-27304-PoC)

reports.first_signal: DOMPurify 3.1.2 or earlier with the default config (SVG and MathML allowed by default); output re-parsed after sanitize (`innerHTML` re-assignment, a double `sanitize()` as in older Mermaid, or a server-side pre-parse); a Chromium or Safari victim, since most variants do not work in Firefox

In an isolated copy, check whether sanitized output changes structurally after one extra `DOMParser` round-trip with a harmless marker
PoCs use `alert(1)` only

reports.first_signal: A sensitive action reachable by top-level navigation with attacker-chosen parameters (OAuth authorize, account settings); a single-click confirm with a predictable button position; buttons live immediately on load with no gesture gating
reports.mechanic: A `window.open` decoy, `window.opener.location` navigating the parent tab to a sensitive page, and the decoy closing on `mousedown` so the second click lands on the real button.
chain: Open the decoy with `window.open`
Navigate the parent tab with `window.opener.location` to the target action
Close the decoy on `mousedown` so the second click of a double-click lands on the real button
reports.impact_proof: Account takeover demonstrated on Salesforce and Slack; claimed on "almost every site that supports OAuth", crypto wallets and extensions. X-Frame-Options, CSP frame-ancestors and SameSite Lax/Strict are all irrelevant because the target loads top-level in the victim's session.
keywords: top-level navigation in the victim session

reports.first_signal: A user-controlled value (fragment, query, path parameter or stored data) appearing as a path SEGMENT in front-end API URLs; sinks keep the original method, headers and body, so every finding is described as a source-sink pair

Record the source-sink pair with its method, header and body constraints

Chain a GET sink plus a file upload or download gadget hosting crafted JSON (a `%PDF` header within the first 1024 bytes still parses as JSON for mmmagic; WebP/JSON polyglots) into a state-changing POST
reports.impact_proof: Mattermost, Rocket.Chat and others; JSONP-to-XSS and CSPT-to-XSS variants collected in the resources post.
keywords: user input as a path segment

reports.first_signal: Subdomains hosting user content or any subdomain XSS (self-XSS is enough); a cookie-based session WITHOUT the `__Host-` prefix; state-changing JSON endpoints relying on a CORS preflight with no CSRF token; multi-step connect or payment flows. SameSite is irrelevant because a subdomain is same-site.

chain: Two own accounts plus your own subdomain
Set a parent-domain cookie with a narrow Path
Verify that the endpoint acts under the planted session while other pages keep the real one
The victim's OAuth link lands on the attacker's account
reports.impact_proof: Gitpod CVE-2024-21583: the victim's Bitbucket/GitHub account linked to the attacker's account, giving repo access, source edit and commits.
keywords: identity link lands on attacker account

reports.first_signal: Callback error handling that redirects based on `Referer`; a behaviour change when callback parameters are stripped; a token appearing in the fragment after changing `response_type`; providers accepting a multi-value `response_type` or `prompt=none`; no interactive final step

chain: With your own account, strip or alter callback parameters and record the redirect target
Swap `response_type`; `response_type=code,id_token` (Google accepts comma-separated) returns the usable code too
Open the flow via `window.open` from your own page and read the Referer the callback sees; `prompt=none` removes the account picker so nothing interactive breaks the chain
reports.impact_proof: Full account takeover via a stolen `code` plus `state`; about $3,000, with CVSS reduced to roughly 7.7 because not all users link Google.

reports.first_signal: Cross-origin responses whose size or host differs by authentication state
reports.mechanic: Two XS-leak oracles: Chrome connection-pool prioritisation leaks a cross-domain redirect's hostname, and chained edge cases leak a cross-origin response's size through ETag length.
chain: Pick a cross-origin response whose size or host varies with auth state
Measure it with the connection-pool priority oracle, or with the ETag length oracle
reports.impact_proof: Low direct bounty value, high value as oracles; the panel rated the ETag length leak more versatile and harder to patch than the redirect leak.

reports.bounty: six figures across fintech, crypto and e-commerce programs
reports.first_signal: Next.js 13.5.1 to 14.2.9, pages router, non-dynamic SSR routes, NOT on Vercel; the buildId visible in `__NEXT_DATA__`; the tell is Cache-Control flipping from `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate` to `s-maxage=1, stale-while-revalidate` when the header is added
reports.mechanic: An external `x-now-route-matches` makes Next.js treat an SSR response as SSG, so the framework's own cache stores it with `s-maxage=1, stale-while-revalidate`; combined with a data request (`__nextDataReq`, `/_next/data/{buildID}/page.json`, `x-nextjs-data`) the JSON gets cached under the HTML URL.
chain: Add `x-now-route-matches` to a non-dynamic SSR route and require the Cache-Control flip
Pair it with a data request so JSON is cached under the HTML URL

Use an unimportant endpoint only: cache busters barely work because the poisoned cache is internal; for the external-cache variant drop `Accept-Encoding` if it is in the cache key, since browsers always send it so real users are unaffected

reports.mechanic: The `x-middleware-subrequest` recursion guard, sent externally, skips middleware entirely (CVE-2025-29927, CVSS 9.1).
chain: Request the gated path with and without the header and compare
Payload by version: `pages/_middleware` below 12.2; `middleware` or `src/middleware` on 12.2 and later; the name repeated at least 5 times colon-separated on 13.2 and later
The redirect or rewrite disappears and the CSP header vanishes; avoid CDN-fronted paths because a 404 can get cached (CPDoS)
reports.impact_proof: Authorization bypass (15.1.7), CSP bypass (15.0.3) and cache-poisoning DoS. All versions from 11.1.4 up to the patches 15.2.3 / 14.2.25 / 13.5.9 / 12.3.5.

reports.first_signal: `_next/static` in the body or "Next.js" in the headers, then internal `href` paths regex-extracted from the page
reports.mechanic: A reusable three-request detection flow for CVE-2025-29927: fingerprint, baseline for middleware involvement, then require a blocked-to-200 transition.

Baseline: keep only paths showing middleware involvement (`x-middleware-rewrite`/`-next`/`-redirect`, or a Location containing `unauthorized`) AND status not 200
Exploit: resend with both 5x payloads and require the transition blocked to 200

Require HTTP 500 with `E{"digest"` in the body
Note the caveats: a digest error without THIS payload does not count, the probe can over-flag outside the affected version range, and WAFs often block the full RCE payload but not this probe
reports.impact_proof: Pre-auth RCE; scanner github.com/assetnote/react2shell-scanner.

Inject CLI arguments through the query string
Load a Twig template over the FTP wrapper for pre-auth RCE

Enumerate the products that import it
Reach an RCE sink in each

reports.first_signal: The SSRF follows redirects; the error text CHANGES with the redirect count (a JSON parse error at low counts, `NetworkException` past the maximum); the full response leaks for some status codes such as 500 but not for 200

chain: Stand up an own Flask redirect-loop server with incrementing statuses ending at a harmless page
If the chain plus the final body appear in the error, the target is susceptible
Only then aim at internal endpoints, with authorization
reports.impact_proof: AWS metadata credentials retrieved; the author reports reuse "in several situations". Found black-box before the binary finished loading in Ghidra.

reports.first_signal: Which of a pair returns first; DNS cache warming; a 64-octet DNS label makes resolution be skipped and so run faster; exceptions short-circuit slow paths ("timing attacks are exceptionally good at detecting exceptions"); keyed versus unkeyed parameter at 310ms versus 22ms; WAF delay stacking on repeated parameters

chain: Send probe pairs: `'` versus `''`; `%23` versus `%21` for server-side parameter pollution; invalid versus valid JSON escape; a random header versus `True-Client-IP: <own domain>`; a duplicate Host; `aaa{62}` versus `aaa{63}`
Take 30 measurements per input and compare bottom quartiles
Report at 80% or better consistent ordering over up to 50 pairs
reports.impact_proof: On a 30,000-site bed: 375 IP-spoofing-vulnerable domains; blind SQLi; blind JSON injection; hundreds of reverse proxies exposing tens of thousands of internal routes; firewall bypass to an internal SonarQube; staging and a US government admin console; 403 turned into access. Smallest exploited gap 200 microseconds.

The login page loads `/assets/_js/`; ffuf it to find `login.js` and extract `/forgotPassword/resetPassword.json`, which takes an email plus a new password and no token
`/adminProfile/getSecurityQuestion.json` is an account-existence oracle; employee names from LinkedIn as `<initial><lastname>@subaru.com`, valid on the 4th guess
Custom 2FA was a UI modal only - delete the line and the backend still serves
